sizeCaveats.headline: 763.9 MiB (801,003,729 bytes) across 76,295 files, from a single-pass file walk on a CLEAN npm ci --omit=dev tree before anything was installed on top of it. THIS is the measured figure.
sizeCaveats.retracted: A later `du -sh` reported 939M node_modules / 3.2G total. The builder RETRACTED it rather than reporting it: that du was still walking the tree when the dev-dependency install for the standalone experiment started in the same directory, so it read a tree mid-transition from pruned to full, and the 3.2G total includes dev deps plus the finished .next build. Retracting a number you could have led with is the behaviour I want; a wrong size here sets a wrong threshold for 23-S2 and 23-S3.
sizeCaveats.caveat1_logicalNotDisk: 763.9 MiB is a LOGICAL byte sum, not disk allocation. 76,295 mostly-small files cost meaningfully more on disk because of 4K block rounding. The tarball 23-S2 builds compresses logical bytes, so 763.9 MiB is the right number for ARTIFACT SIZE; the on-disk footprint after extraction on the VPS will be larger, and the release-size threshold in the DoD must not be set from the artifact number.
sizeCaveats.caveat2_win32: It is a WIN32 tree. The Linux artifact swaps @img/sharp-win32-x64, @napi-rs/canvas-win32-x64-msvc, @next/swc-win32-x64-msvc and the two @rollup/rollup-win32-* packages for linux-x64-gnu equivalents, and Linux sharp additionally pulls @img/sharp-libvips-linux-x64. Expect the Linux production tree to be LARGER. 23-S2 must RE-MEASURE on the ubuntu-latest runner rather than inherit this number.
sizeCaveats.consequence: 23-S2's brief must carry both caveats explicitly, or it will inherit a win32 logical-byte figure as if it were a Linux on-disk one.

standingPractices.rule: Every PR body must LABEL which half of a red-then-green proof is CI-proven and which is local-only. A local red presented beside a CI green reads as one continuous proof and is not one.

standingPractices.rule: A guard for a write path gets BOTH a cheap-job guard (drive the real function, assert what it passes) and a real-database guard (prove the database accepts it) whenever both are cheap. They are different claims: what the code asks for, versus what Postgres accepts.
standingPractices.why: A guard that lives only in the integration job is one `if:`, one early-failing step or one allow-list omission away from not running - which is exactly #489, #507 and #556's wiring gap.
